BCG Institute modeling of 54 countries and 47 industries challenges the assumption that manufacturing must keep shifting to lower-cost economies. Technology—more than tariffs or energy policy—could let established hubs retain production, provided companies and governments modernize before factories and skills migrate elsewhere.

Without modernization, traditional hubs face a large production exodusIf current cost disadvantages persist, the US, Western Europe, and Japan could lose $1.8 trillion in manufacturing value added, putting 26 million direct and indirect manufacturing-related jobs at risk.

Factories of the future can reverse the labor-cost equationAgentic systems and AI-powered robotics could raise labor productivity 2.5x, making automation and proximity to customers more valuable than low wages—especially where shipping costs erase the remaining offshore advantage.

Tariffs can buy time, but cannot create durable competitivenessHigh tariffs may retain manufacturing activity at current productivity levels, but they raise costs and lose value as factories improve. With fivefold productivity gains, protectionism reduces Western Europe’s potential output by $315 billion.

Leaders must pair technology investment with energy, skills, and footprint decisionsAutomation can narrow energy disadvantages, but cannot eliminate them in power-intensive sectors. Manufacturers should modernize plants before relocation becomes irreversible, while policymakers strengthen digital infrastructure, workforce skills, and affordable electricity.

The story of global manufacturing has been told so often that its trajectory now seems inevitable: production has steadily shifted toward China and, to a lesser extent, India, while traditional manufacturing hubs in the US, Western Europe, and Japan have lost ground. BCG Institute modeling suggests that 26 million jobs located there could move overseas if competitive disadvantages remain in place.But that outcome is not inevitable. Technology, geopolitics, and energy costs are challenging the economic rationale behind decades of production decisions, and they could redraw the manufacturing map. Of these factors, technology has the greatest potential to transform manufacturing competitiveness. Recent breakthroughs in agentic systems and physical AI can turn factories into hyperproductive factories of the future (FoF), eventually delivering up to 2.5 times the labor productivity of conventional factories and narrowing—or even reversing—the cost advantages that have drawn production to lower-cost countries.These developments do not mean that jobs must be lost to automation. Our analysis suggests that the productivity gains from FoF could help traditional manufacturing hubs retain production and employment that might otherwise move abroad. Factory jobs will change as automation advances, but the greater employment risk may come from failing to modernize and thus making it harder for domestic manufacturers to compete with lower-cost producers.For manufacturers, the critical task is to identify where investments in new technology could make their factories more competitive and how instability in trade conditions and energy costs might affect those decisions. For policymakers, it is to determine how to enhance local competitiveness over the long term through measures that support business investment in FoF technology, such as improving skills and digital infrastructure.How Technology, Geopolitics, and Access to Affordable Energy Shape the Global Manufacturing Map
Explore how technology, geopolitics, and energy evolution reshape the allocation of $16 trillion of manufacturing value in 2025 US dollars added across regions.

The Evolution of Manufacturing Competitiveness
Over the past 25 years, the geography of manufacturing has changed dramatically. Since 2000, China’s share of global manufacturing value added (MVA) has risen by 28 percentage points and India’s by 2, while the US and Western Europe have each lost 11 points and Japan 5. In traditional manufacturing hubs (the US, Western Europe, and Japan), productivity has failed to keep pace with wage growth, eroding these region’s cost competitiveness. High energy prices in Europe and Japan have compounded the disadvantage. At the same time, China has strengthened its industrial ecosystem and improved its infrastructure and workforce capabilities, enhancing its attractiveness as a manufacturing location.BCG Institute’s modeling suggests that if these trends persist, about $1.8 trillion in MVA produced in the traditional hubs could move overseas, putting an estimated 26 million manufacturing-related jobs at risk. Western Europe accounts for the largest share of both ($991 billion and 15 million jobs), followed by the US ($460 billion and 5 million jobs) and Japan ($314 billion and 6 million jobs). (See Exhibit 1.)

To examine whether these trends can be reversed, we analyzed manufacturing competitiveness across 54 countries and 47 industries, which collectively account for more than 95% of global MVA. (see the sidebar, “How the Manufacturing Competitiveness Advisor Tool Works.”) Our research considered how advances in technology, geopolitical developments, and energy costs could affect the location of manufacturing activity. However, these three forces differ in their potential impact. We modeled how the traditional hubs’ combined MVA would change as each force varied across its full scenario range, holding the other two constant. We found that technology is the only force that could lift the traditional hubs’ MVA above today’s level. (See Exhibit 2). Tariffs and energy costs could offset some of the losses, but neither could reverse them. Technology could also change how much those other two factors matter.

How the Manufacturing Competitiveness Advisor Tool Works

BCG developed the Manufacturing Competitiveness Advisor Tool to assess how technological progress, changing trade policies, and energy costs could alter the global distribution of manufacturing. The model covers 54 countries that account for more than 95% of global manufacturing value added (MVA) across 47 industrial sectors.The analysis starts with the approximately $16 trillion in global MVA recorded in 2025 and simulates how that existing activity could be redistributed as manufacturing conditions change. It assumes that any production capable of relocating will move immediately to a more competitive location. The model does not forecast growth in global manufacturing or predict when actual relocations might occur.How the Model WorksThe analysis consists of three steps:Determine how much production can relocate. The model estimates movable MVA by sector, country, and customer market, recognizing that some production must remain close to customers and that cost differences alone do not determine whether relocation is feasible. Estimates of the movable share by sector draw on a BCG Institute survey of 1,000 manufacturing executives.Assess the competitiveness of potential locations. Each location receives a score from 1 (very low) to 10 (very high), based on a weighted assessment of 42 cost and qualitative factors. The assessment reflects the sector, customer market, and type of manufacturing asset. Factor weighting also draws on the survey of manufacturing executives.Simulate the redistribution of manufacturing activity. The model allocates movable MVA to the highest-scoring locations in proportion to their competitiveness scores for each manufacturing activity.How the Scenarios Are ConstructedThe model combines different assumptions about three forces that influence manufacturing competitiveness:Technology. The model considers five levels of labor productivity relative to today's baseline: current (1.0×), incremental (2.0×), medium (2.5×), accelerated (3.3×), and radical (5.0×). These productivity levels correspond to reductions in labor requirements of 0%, 50%, 60%, 70%, and 80%, respectively. The current scenario assumes that recent AI breakthroughs do not scale. The incremental scenario reflects limited adoption, and the medium scenario assumes that factories achieve the productivity of today’s early AI adopters through more extensive redesign. The accelerated and radical scenarios envision increasingly capable robotics and automation, culminating in factories that require very little human labor.Trade. Four scenarios range from duty-free global trade to the current tariff structure and two levels of increased protectionism. Under the status quo, US tariffs remain around 10% to 15% across sectors. The medium scenario raises tariffs by 10 percentage points on trading partners and by 15 percentage points on rivals. The high-tariff scenario raises them by 25 and 80 percentage points, respectively. The model measured increases against September 2026 rates.Energy. Three scenarios examine changes in industrial electricity prices relative to the end of 2025. Under convergence, prices fall by 50% in energy-vulnerable regions and by 15% in regions with intermediate exposure, but they remain unchanged in energy-rich regions. Under the status quo, existing differences persist. Under divergence, prices rise by 40% in vulnerable regions and fall by 20% in energy-rich regions. The divergence scenario also quadruples the weight assigned to access to critical raw materials in the competitiveness assessment.How to Interpret the ResultsThese scenarios are simulations, not forecasts. They illustrate how the existing distribution of MVA could change under different competitive conditions, rather than predicting how much production will actually relocate or when. The simulations also hold existing trade imbalances and exchange rates constant, excluding potential adjustments that could affect the geographic distribution of manufacturing.

The Factory of the Future Redefines Global Competitiveness
The FoF has long promised to transform manufacturing through automation. Two recent technological breakthroughs are bringing that ambition closer to reality. Agentic systems can support largely autonomous operations, while physical AI enables robots to perform an expanding range of tasks. Advances in computing power and the integration of factory operations with digital systems and data are making these technologies increasingly practical to deploy at industrial scale. The scope of work that manufacturers can automate has expanded by 50% in just three years, and FoF has the potential to achieve up to 2.5 times the labor productivity of conventional operations. Although it will take time—potentially decades—for these technologies to gain widespread adoption and for manufacturers in high-cost countries to fully realize the gains, that improvement could make upgrading an existing plant more economical than relocating abroad.The benefits are likely to vary considerably by industry. Two factors will determine whether the FoF can make production in high-cost countries competitive: the potential for automation and the cost of transporting finished goods to customers. Automation can narrow the disadvantage of manufacturing in high-wage countries, but shipping expenses often play a decisive role in tipping the advantage toward or away from local production. When the remaining difference is smaller than the logistics costs of importing goods from a lower-cost country, manufacturing closer to customers becomes the cheaper option. Where automation offers fewer savings and transportation costs are low, offshore production retains its advantage. (See Exhibit 3.)

Still, achieving the productivity gains from automation requires more than new technology. Manufacturers also need skilled workers, strong digital infrastructure, and the flexibility to reorganize their operations and retrain employees.As automation reduces the labor required to make goods, wage scales become less important in determining where manufacturing is most economical. Technology can also reduce waste and make more efficient use of energy and materials, further narrowing the cost gap. As a result, qualitative factors, including infrastructure and workforce capabilities—areas in which traditional manufacturing hubs such as Western Europe remain strong—carry greater weight.To assess how shifts in competitiveness could redraw the manufacturing map, we modeled the potential redistribution of the $16 trillion in global MVA recorded in 2025 (in real dollar terms) under productivity scenarios ranging from no improvement to a radical fivefold increase in labor productivity, equivalent to an 80% reduction in labor intensity. This last scenario goes well beyond the improvement of 2.5 times generally considered achievable in a FoF. It assumes further, uninterrupted progress in robotics, physical AI, and agentic systems.The results suggest how dramatically the manufacturing map could change. As noted earlier, without productivity gains, the traditional hubs could lose $1.8 trillion in MVA. But under the most optimistic technology scenario, with its fivefold increase in labor productivity, they could gain approximately $2.3 trillion compared with the no-gain scenario, more than offsetting that projected loss. Western Europe would gain an estimated $1,663 billion, the US $320 billion, and Japan $275 billion. (See Exhibit 4.)

How the Factory of the Future May Impact Jobs
Increased automation in industry often raises concerns about job losses, and these concerns are heightened in traditional manufacturing hubs, where employers have struggled with rising costs. BCG Institute’s modeling suggests, however, that the real choice facing these regions is not between today’s employment and an automated future, but between modernizing factories and losing them. A more automated FoF could help traditional manufacturing hubs preserve employment that would otherwise be lost as production moved abroad.This is possible because automation can make local manufacturing more competitive, reducing the incentive to relocate factories abroad. Although automated factories need fewer workers to produce the same output, greater competitiveness could help a region expand its industrial base and create additional jobs. In addition, protecting domestic manufacturing preserves the wider network of indirect jobs, such as in supplier and service networks, and can stimulate broad-based economic activity, creating employment in other sectors.Our model of Western Europe illustrates the difference. Without productivity improvements, direct and indirect manufacturing employment could fall from approximately 42 million to 27.6 million as production shifts to more competitive locations abroad. With productivity gains, the outcome depends on how far technology advances. If factories become 2.5 times more productive, more production stays in the region. Because hyperproductive factories need fewer workers, employment reaches only 34.9 million, which is still below today’s level. Only in our most optimistic technology scenario, with factories five times more productive, does employment recover to about 40 million as Western Europe captures an increasing share of global MVA. That number increases to 40 million to 45 million once jobs created elsewhere in the economy are counted, as higher productivity raises incomes and spending. (See Exhibit 5.)

But the timing of deploying hyperproductive factories matters, too. If production moves abroad before the technology is widely adopted, it may never return. Reestablishing manufacturing capacity after factories have closed or relocated can be far more difficult than retaining it in the first place.And even when factories stay, preserving manufacturing employment does not mean keeping the work itself the same. Indeed, many factory jobs will disappear, while others will change substantially as workers take on new responsibilities in hyperproductive factories, such as supervising robotic systems, training robots, and resolving problems that automated equipment cannot handle. Filling these jobs will require retraining on an industrial scale, as manufacturers invest in their workers, prepare them for new careers, and hire people with AI expertise, and as policymakers support the education and skills programs necessary for a more automated industrial economy.Geopolitics: Trade Protection Cannot Replace Competitiveness
Governments today are intervening more actively in manufacturing decisions, often in the name of economic security. Industrial policy measures motivated by such concerns have increased more than sixfold since 2022. Tariffs are the most visible instrument, but subsidies, export controls, investment screening, and local-content requirements contribute to altering the economics of production as well, particularly in sectors such as semiconductors, metals, and rare earths. In a 2025 BCG Institute survey of 1,000 manufacturing executives, 90% said that tariffs above 25% would make exporting uneconomical. The same survey ranked geopolitical risk fourth among manufacturers’ leading challenges, up from sixth in 2022. Manufacturers are also turning to regional supply chains to reduce their exposure to trade disruptions.Trade protection can help countries retain manufacturing activity when their producers cannot compete on cost. By raising the price of imports, tariffs can make domestic production more economical than sourcing goods from abroad. Our model illustrates the potential effect of such efforts. Assuming that manufacturing productivity remains at today’s levels, high tariffs would keep an estimated $688 billion in MVA in Western Europe, $552 billion in the US, and $251 billion in Japan that would otherwise shift to other regions under a free trade scenario. (See Exhibit 6.)

But policymakers must balance the benefits of protective trade policies against their potential impact on broader economic growth. Although they can safeguard domestic production and employment, such policies can also raise costs for manufacturers and consumers, limit exports as countries reciprocate with their own protectionist measures, and reduce the pressure on companies to improve their productivity and compete globally. And because the protections depend on government policy, they may be short-lived as trade agreements and political priorities change.As factories become more productive, however, the calculation changes. Manufacturers that can hold their own internationally have less need for trade protections and more to gain from access to foreign markets. In Western Europe, the model shows that the manufacturing value protected by tariffs falls from $688 billion without productivity gains to approximately $465 billion with medium productivity gains. With a fivefold increase in productivity, high tariffs actually reduce the region’s potential MVA by $315 billion compared with open trade. (See Exhibit 7.) Our model finds a similar pattern in the US and Japan. These simulations hold existing trade imbalances and exchange rates constant; changes in either could affect the results.

The implications extend beyond tariffs themselves. Persistent global trade imbalances are a broader problem that may require a coordinated, multilateral response. Although there is no simple solution, countries need not wait for one: investing in technology to improve manufacturing competitiveness is something they can do on their own.Energy Costs: A New Dividing Line That Technology Can Narrow
Countries that depend heavily on imported energy face a growing cost disadvantage in manufacturing compared with countries that have abundant domestic supplies. Geopolitical conflicts and global energy policies are unpredictable, which exposes producers in energy-importing countries to volatile markets. Meanwhile, electrification and the rapid expansion of AI data centers increase demand for electricity, putting additional pressure on industrial power supplies and prices.Since 2010, industrial electricity has become more expensive in most major manufacturing regions, for several reasons. Supply has struggled to keep pace with rising demand, heavy grid investment has been passed on to users, and market rules designed for periods of flat demand and falling costs have pushed prices higher. Import-dependent regions face the highest industrial electricity prices of all. In 2025, manufacturers in Western Europe, where prices have risen by more than 50% since 2010, paid roughly two and a half to three times as much for industrial electricity as manufacturers in the US and China, and Japanese manufacturers about twice as much. (See Exhibit 8.) Because the price of natural gas often determines electricity prices, Western Europe was particularly exposed to the 2022 gas shock, and prices still remain well above precrisis levels. Rising network costs, taxes, and levies, spread across declining industrial demand, have added to the burden.

Import dependency is best read as a directional indicator, however. The metric includes oil imports, which have little bearing on power generation, whereas reliance on imported gas and coal and the availability of domestic renewables and nuclear power are more directly linked to electricity costs.Germany provides a useful example of what is at stake. Our model finds that about $290 billion of German MVA is at risk of relocating if the current competitiveness gap persists. But this is not simply a question of factory productivity. With industrial electricity prices comparable to those in the US and China, $110 billion of German MVA could match the costs of China-based competitors that serve the German market. High energy costs already influence investment decisions: roughly one-third of German industrial manufacturers are moving production capacity abroad because of energy prices, as are nearly one in ten UK manufacturers.Those decisions may prove well-founded if regional prices continue to diverge. We modeled two possibilities: one in which energy prices converge as countries develop renewable energy, reform wholesale electricity markets, and reduce their dependence on imported fuels; and another in which growing electricity demand and supply disruptions widen the disparities. If no improvement were to occur in manufacturing labor productivity, our model finds that China would gain $407 billion more in MVA under the divergence scenario than under convergence. The US would gain $151 billion, while Western Europe would lose $173 billion and Japan $95 billion. These figures represent differences in the geographic allocation of existing manufacturing activity, not additional global production. (See Exhibit 9.)

The effects would also vary considerably within regions. In Europe, countries with relatively inexpensive hydroelectric or nuclear power, particularly in the Nordic region, would be better positioned than Germany and the UK.Technology, however, could change how much these energy cost differences matter to manufacturers. By reducing labor requirements and making more efficient use of energy and materials, automation could offset some of the cost disadvantages that manufacturers in countries with expensive energy face. In our medium productivity scenario, which also assumes more efficient energy use, the gap in Western Europe’s MVA between the energy-divergence and energy-convergence scenarios narrows from approximately $173 billion to $77 billion. (See Exhibit 10.) In our most optimistic technology scenario, with even greater improvements in both labor and resource productivity, the difference virtually disappears. Japan follows a similar pattern The model examines different electricity-price scenarios but does not account for how additional demand from AI data centers could affect those prices.

In any event, technology cannot eliminate the importance of affordable, reliable energy. In energy-intensive industries, such as steel and chemicals, electricity costs may still determine where production is economically viable, even in highly automated factories. And the technology itself exerts additional pressure on electricity supplies. In the US, data centers accounted for 46% of total market charges across PJM’s last four capacity auctions, as prices rose from $29 per megawatt-day to more than $300 per megawatt-day. Manufacturers therefore face the double challenge of using technology to offset high energy costs while competing with that same technology for increasingly expensive electricity.What Manufacturers and Policymakers Can Do
The combined effects of technology, trade policies, and energy costs require manufacturers to reconsider where and how they produce goods. For their part, policymakers need to determine how best to sustain manufacturing activity and employment over the long term. Both can take a number of useful specific steps.Manufacturers:Assess the vulnerability of manufacturing networks. Examine how technological progress, changing trade policies, and energy costs—individually and in combination—might affect the economics and resilience of existing production footprints.Make technology and footprint decisions together. Determine what level of FoF modernization would render each location competitive and when upgrading a plant that is already online makes more economic sense than moving production elsewhere.Plan for long-term competitiveness, not the latest disruption. Consider how the timing of technology investments could affect future production costs, and weigh those decisions against longer-term trade and energy risks. Avoid making costly, difficult-to-reverse investments in response to temporary disruptions.Policymakers:Understand how the three forces interact. Use scenario analysis to assess how different combinations of technological progress, trade policies, and energy costs could affect regional competitiveness, manufacturing activity, and employment. Policies that protect factories in one scenario may prove ineffective or even counterproductive in another.Invest in the foundations of lasting competitiveness. Accelerate the adoption of FoF technologies, strengthen workforce skills and digital infrastructure, and ensure that the costs of expanding electricity grids to accommodate AI and electrification do not fall disproportionately on industrial users.Protect strategic sectors where technology alone cannot close the cost gap. For industries that supply essential materials for defense, infrastructure, or technology—such as steel, chemicals, and cement—resilience may justify local production even in situations where FoF investment cannot make the operation economically viable on its own. Policymakers can condition such support on modernization, so that protection does not weaken the manufacturer’s incentive to improve productivity.

Technology has the potential to alter the economics that have governed manufacturing location decisions for decades. But its impact will depend on how it interacts with trade policies and energy costs as well as on how quickly manufacturers and governments respond. With global MVA potentially rising from $16 trillion today to $26 trillion by 2050, the decisions that manufacturers and policymakers made now will help determine where that growth takes place.
